h: פָּרָשַׁת שְׁקָלִים, מַאֲמָר ג׳ Parshas Shekalim — Maamar Gimmel

p: In the Pesikta (end of section 10, siman 15):
"This one He lowers and this one He raises:
the 'this' that lowered Israel to the pit of destruction
the one that raises their horn by it,
The meaning is not that he derives a gezeirah shavah
as we have said several times,
that the thing is plainly before one's eyes,
so that one can point with a finger and say "this";
and likewise when it is engraved in the heart,
for since they are engraved on the tablet of his heart,
it is as though plainly before the eye,
And this is what they meant by "this one He lowers":
in that Israel said of the Calf
which shows that they did not say it
it was engraved in their heart—
עַל יְדֵי זֶה הִשְׁפִּילָם לִבְאֵר שַׁחַת
through this He lowered them to the pit of destruction.
their horn was repaired and raised
through the words "This they shall give."
For in truth one must understand
and what is written in the Pesikta
that Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, wondered,
"Who can give a ransom for his soul?"
and he thought it would be like a talent,
or a hundred or fifty pieces of silver,
it would have sufficed to tell him
that they should give ten gerah,
and he would know the coin;
so why did He show it to him?
But the explanation is as they said
He took from beneath the Throne of Glory
and showed him: 'This they shall give,'"
how a redemption of money could help,
something like a coin of fire,
is only the love and the generosity,
in the manner of what is written
"Its flashes are flashes of fire, etc.;
many waters, etc.," said of love.
on the contrary, a small coin suffices,
even for a very wealthy man.
the greater the love and the longing,
that he merited that the King of kings would accept
And this is why they said "from beneath the Throne of Glory":
between the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר חֵלֶק ב קלה, ב)
in the mystery of One," etc.
And this is the meaning of "This they shall give":
that the main thing is that they give the longing and the love,
that the love of Hashem be engraved
upon the tablet of their heart,
until it is plain to the eye,
as though pointed to with a finger.
And this is what they meant by "and this one He raises":
that He raised their horn through "this,"
that is, through the generosity and love for Hashem
that was engraved on the tablet of their heart.
to fulfill the mitzvah of shekalim in practice,
and every single Jew yearns to fulfill it;
and if it were possible to fulfill it,
so that his shekel would reach the Mikdash;
and from this longing actual shekalim are made,
and it raises the horn of Israel.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 10 — “When David saw that through this they had atonement, he began saying: Come and see the wonders of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His works: through the very thing with which they angered Him, He provided atonement for them. For God judges: this He lowers and this He raises. This that lowered Israel to the pit of destruction was This is your god; and this that raises Israel, lifting their horn, is This they shall give.” Rav Tzadok explains the repeated demonstrative this as something vividly present to the heart; he does not treat the exposition as a formal legal gezerah shavah.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Taanis 31a — “In the future the Holy One will make a circle for the tzaddikim … and each one will point with his finger, as it says: ‘Behold, this is our God, we hoped for Him.’” This is the source of the rule Rav Tzadok says he has stated many times: “zeh” is said of what is so revealed that one can point to it with a finger.

paragraphs.text: Megillah 15b — “And all this is worth nothing to me teaches that all the treasures of that wicked man were engraved upon his heart. Whenever he saw Mordechai sitting at the king's gate, he said: All this is worth nothing to me.” The Gemara describes Haman's wealth as inwardly present to him. Rav Tzadok draws from the wording a general explanation of the demonstrative this; he does not endorse Haman's attachment to wealth.

paragraphs.text: Pesikta Rabbati 16, exposition of “They shall give a ransom for their souls” — “Rabbi Yehudah bar Simon said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: Moses heard three things from the Almighty and was alarmed and recoiled. ... When they sinned, and it was said, ‘Each shall give a ransom for his soul,’ Moses said: Master of the worlds, who can give the ransom of his soul? ‘A man cannot redeem his brother; he cannot give God his ransom; the redemption of their souls is costly.’ The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: It is not as you suppose; rather, ‘This they shall give’—they shall give something like this. Rabbi Meir said: The Holy One, blessed be He, brought out something like a coin of fire from beneath the Throne of Glory, showed it to Moses, and said to him: ‘This they shall give’—they shall give something like this.” The requested chapter contains the fiery coin and the seemingly impossible ransom. The detailed alternative monetary amounts cited here belong to the Tanchuma versions. The digital witness presents chapter 16 as a single text, so the manuscript’s subsection 7 has not been separately collated.

paragraphs.text: Bamidbar Rabbah 12:3 — “When the Holy One, blessed be He, said: Each shall give a ransom for his soul, Moshe said: Who could give the ransom of his soul? ... Rabbi Meir said: The Holy One, blessed be He, took something like a coin of fire from beneath the Throne of Glory and showed it to Moshe: This they shall give; like this they shall give.” The fiery coin is the Midrash's image. Rav Tzadok interprets its fire as the love and generosity accompanying the gift, rather than as the value of the metal.

paragraphs.text: Song of Songs 8:6-7 — “Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death, jealousy fierce as the grave; its flashes are flashes of fire, a mighty flame. Many waters cannot extinguish love, nor can rivers sweep it away. If a man offered all the wealth of his house for love, he would be utterly scorned.” The verses join the seal upon the heart, fire, love, and the inability of wealth to buy love. These images explain why the small monetary gift can express an inward devotion greater than its price.

paragraphs.text: Parallel: Sod Yesharim, Parshas Shekalim 1 — “The half-shekel shows that Yisrael recognize they have no completeness without Hashem, and Hashem too says there is no completeness in the glory of Heaven without Yisrael's service; the joining is called a whole shekel.” The Radziner, following the Zohar Chadash on Ki Sisa, makes the half-shekel itself the sign of this union, each side a half that the other completes.

paragraphs.text: Zohar, Terumah 14 — “The mystery of Shabbos is Shabbos united in the mystery of one, so that the mystery of one may rest upon her. The prayer of Shabbos eve is offered when the precious holy Throne has been united in the mystery of one and has been prepared so that the supernal Holy King may rest upon it.” This is the Shabbos passage also recited as Kegavna. Rav Tzadok draws its image of a throne prepared through unity into his explanation of the coin taken from beneath the Throne of Glory.
